deep.reconstruction:
Setting (cote 154, 1983-84). Grothendieck studies systems of pseudo-lines Σ = {D_1,…,D_n} in a projective plane or disc X. For each 'relative position' L of an additional pseudo-line with respect to Σ, he builds a 2-dimensional cell complex, essentially a cellular surface. Its cells are polygonal discs indexed by relative positions. Its edges are 'arcs' of incidence, specialisation and generalisation, i.e. moves in which a generic position degenerates into a more special one, or the reverse. A position can be generic, critical, semi-critical/exceptional, or hypercritical.

Previous page: he glued polygonal discs and quadrangular faces along arcs of specialisation and generalisation. Each square face has one specialisation side, one generalisation side and two mixed sides. Faces correspond bijectively to pairs (L, a), with a an incidence arc of specialisation type. He then notes the construction is incomplete. The hypercritical positions, and the arcs going to or from them, were left out, so circles remain free and must be capped by further polygonal discs.

This page, first paragraph. The same gluing procedure, now along the arcs of exceptional specialisation, gives a compact cellular surface with boundary. He encodes it by a combinatorial graph Γ = (S, Ā, σ, τ):
- S is the set of vertices (one per polygon/position).
- Ā is the set of half-edges ('arêtes orientées').
- σ: Ā → S is the incidence map.
- τ is an involution on Ā. Its fixed points are 'free edges', i.e. oriented edges with no other end.
Taking for each s a polygonal disc D_s and identifying sides along the ordinary edges (τā ≠ ā) gives a surface with boundary. The free edges, the fixed points of τ, make up the boundary circles. This is the standard dictionary of 'combinatorial maps with boundary' (vertex/face permutation plus a partial involution).

Second paragraph. The quadrangular holes ('trous quadrangulaires', bounded by circuits of incidence arcs) have already been filled. The remaining holes are bounded by circuits of exceptional-specialisation arcs, which here are the free edges. They are to be filled by discs attached to the hypercritical (exceptional) positions. So one must study these circuits and show how to cap them.

Third paragraph. Strategy: imitate the earlier construction. For a position L = D_i + Σ, where the new line coincides with an existing line D_i, define the disc Δ_L as follows.
- Regard D_i as the line at infinity, so X minus D_i is a disc.
- Consider the residual system Σ̲ = (X, Σ∖{D_i}) of n−1 pseudo-lines in that disc.
- The next page says this gives a combinatorial polygon of order 2(n−1), whose boundary points are the ends of the n−1 lines.
Specialisation and generalisation arcs then become 'pulling' operations on these polygons, with canonical transition isomorphisms Δ_L ≅ Δ_D. The next page ends by noting the trouble: the generalisation arcs at a given D overlap each other.

Purpose. Build a cellular model, presumably a closed surface such as a sphere or projective plane, of the space of all relative positions of one extra pseudo-line with respect to an arrangement. In modern terms this is a cell decomposition of the space of single-element extensions of a rank-3 oriented matroid, and a check of its topology.
errors: No mathematical error on this page; it is programmatic. The gluing claim is standard: polygons glued pairwise along sides, with unpaired sides as boundary, give a compact surface with boundary. A caveat is needed: vertex links must be arcs or circles, which requires the cyclic orderings at vertices to be consistent. This is implicit in calling σ, τ a 'graph' of a cellular surface.

Gap acknowledged by the author: the capping discs for circuits of exceptional-specialisation arcs are not yet constructed. The next page shows the naive generalisation arcs overlap, so the procedure does not extend directly.

ideas.what: Encoding a polygonal cellular surface with boundary by Γ = (S, Ā, σ, τ). Ā is the set of half-edges, σ the incidence map to vertices/polygons, τ an involution whose fixed points are free (boundary) edges. Gluing polygons along non-fixed pairs gives a surface with boundary.
ideas.modern_name: combinatorial maps / hypermaps with boundary (partial involution); ribbon-graph presentation of a polygonal surface
ideas.usually_credited_to: Tutte, Jacques, Cori (combinatorial maps, 1960s-70s); Bryant–Singerman (maps with boundary, 1985)
ideas.where_published: Esquisse d'un programme (1984) discusses maps, cartographic groups and dessins; boundary/free-edge variant unsure

ideas.what: Cellular complex whose cells are relative positions of an added pseudo-line to an arrangement Σ, glued along specialisation/generalisation arcs, aiming at a closed surface model.
ideas.modern_name: extension space of a rank-3 oriented matroid (poset of single-element extensions), cellular/topological model; cf. extension space conjecture
ideas.usually_credited_to: Las Vergnas (single-element extensions, 1978); Sturmfels–Ziegler, 'Extension spaces of oriented matroids' (1993); Mnëv–Ziegler

ideas.what: For L = D_i + Σ, take D_i as the line at infinity. The residual arrangement Σ∖{D_i} in the disc gives a 2(n−1)-gon Δ_L, and specialisation acts on these polygons by 'pulling' an arc across D, with canonical transition isomorphisms.
ideas.modern_name: contraction/deletion of an element in an oriented matroid; the local (link) structure of the extension space at an element, i.e. a polygon of 2(n−1) cocircuits on the contracted rank-2 matroid
ideas.usually_credited_to: standard oriented matroid theory (Bland–Las Vergnas, Folkman–Lawrence 1978)

missed.claim: Around 1983-84 Grothendieck was building, by explicit polygon gluing, a cellular surface model of the space of relative positions (single-element extensions) of a pseudo-line arrangement. Its topology in rank 3 later became the subject of Sturmfels–Ziegler's extension-space work (1993). This page is part of an unpublished, independent approach to that problem, including the boundary-capping difficulty at hypercritical (exceptional) positions.
missed.quote: Ici il s'agit de boucher les trous qui restent, une fois bouchés les "trous quadrangulaires" … qu'il s'agit de recoller suivant les arcs de spécialisation exceptionnelle
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: The connection between these notes and oriented-matroid extension spaces seems not to be documented. A historian or combinatorialist could check whether his explicit cell structure differs from the standard extension-poset order complex. If it does, it might give a smaller, more explicit model.

missed.claim: The capping of circuits of exceptional-specialisation arcs by discs for hypercritical positions is left open on this page. The next page reports overlapping generalisation arcs.
missed.quote: On est donc amené à étudier les circuits formés d'arcs de spécialisation exceptionnelle, et voir comment les boucher.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Whether the program completes to a closed surface (sphere/projective plane) would decide if his construction gives an alternative proof of the rank-3 topology of extension spaces. This is only of moderate interest, since rank 3 is understood.

deep.surprise_reason: The page itself is routine: gluing polygons via a combinatorial-map encoding with a partial involution, plus a plan to cap the remaining holes. Interest comes from the larger unpublished program, which anticipates the study of extension spaces of rank-3 oriented matroids. No finished new result appears here.
